name: The Qur’an
fw: CCSS RL/RI/RH / C3 / IL SS 9–12 / Teaching About Religion
fwnote: The course reads a tradition's texts as literature and as historical sources in a public school, so it cites the reading standards for the band (RL, RI, RH, WHST), C3 history for 6–8, Illinois SS.H 9–12, and one of the six principles in "A Teacher's Guide to Religion in the Public Schools" (First Amendment Center) that the AAR 2010 Guidelines build on; alignment is the course author's judgment, not a certification or an endorsement by any of these bodies.

1.bq: What is the Qur'an, and how do Muslim families read and care for it?
std: Identify the main topic of an informational text and retell its key details.
Know and use text features, such as headings and a table of contents, to locate key facts.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
1.write: Draw or tell: How does a Muslim family care for the Qur'an? Use two things from the unit. You could use Al-Fatiha (1:1-7) or The Ant (27:18). Say what the book says, and say what Muslims believe about it.

ch.t: What the Qur'an Is
ch.bq: What is the Qur'an, and how do Muslim families treat it?
ch.talk: Why do you think Amira's family keeps the green book on the highest shelf?
ch.story: The Green Book on the Top Shelf

l.look: Which book on the table do Muslim families read? How do you know?
Allah is the Arabic word for God. Who is this line talking about?
How are Arabic letters different from the letters you write at school?
Which two languages go the same way as Arabic and English? Find each pair.

l.t: A High Shelf and Clean Hands
l.look: What did the boy do before touching the book? Why do you think he did that?
This line is very short. Why might a short line be easy to learn by heart?
Which building do Muslim families walk into? What book is read inside?
Which sentence would you use in class? Why is it the fair one?

ch.t: Surahs and Ayahs
ch.bq: How is the Qur'an put together, and how do children find their way around it?
ch.talk: Why do you think Yusuf's aunt starts him on the short chapters instead of the long ones?

l.look: Which of these holy books has the most parts? Which has the fewest?
What does the number after the colon tell you? What does the number before it tell you?
What does the surah ask God for? Find the line that asks for something.
What is the drink that comes from the bee? Where does the surah say bees build their homes?
What did the ant want the other ants to do? Why?

l.t: Long Ones First, Short Ones Last
l.look: Which surah has the most ayahs? What happens to the numbers as the surah number gets bigger?
Which drawer does the child open first? What is inside it?

2.bq: How do Muslims tell the story of Muhammad and the first words of the Qur'an?
std: Describe the characters, settings and major events of a story using key details.
Ask and answer who, what, where, when, why and how questions about a story's key details.
Teaching About Religion · aware not accepting
Build students' understanding of religions without pressing them to accept any one.
2.write: Draw and tell: How do Muslims say the first words of the Qur'an came? Use the first lines of surah 96, the story of the blanket, and surah 73:1. Tell what each one says and what Muslims say it means.

ch.t: A Boy in Mecca
ch.bq: Who was Muhammad, and what was his life like before the Qur'an?
ch.talk: What would you like to see if a line of camels came to your town?

l.look: What do you notice about how the people move around the Kaaba?
What two seasons does this surah name for the trips?
Which of these happened longest ago?
Who do Muslims say this verse is talking about?
What does a shepherd have to be good at? Name one thing.
Why did the cloth make the families stop arguing?
How many years passed between his marriage and the first words?
Why might a person go to a quiet place like this?

ch.t: The Cave and the Word "Read"
ch.bq: How do Muslims say the first words of the Qur'an came to Muhammad?
ch.talk: Khadijah listened first and then spoke kind words. Why does that help a scared person?

l.look: What does this surah say the angels do on that night?
These lines say God taught people to use something. What is it?
What did Muhammad ask for first when he got home?
Why do Muslims connect this surah to the story of the blanket?
Where did the words come for more years, Mecca or Medina?
Have you ever learned a song by heart? How did you do it?
What are some ways people in your family show respect when they talk about someone?

3.bq: What words and stories from the Qur'an are part of a Muslim child's every day?
std: Retell stories with key details and show you understand their central message or lesson.
Compare two versions of the same story told by different authors or from different cultures.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
3.write: Pick one story from this unit: Nuh's boat, Yunus and the fish, Musa in the basket, or the ant. Draw or write what happens. Tell where it is in the Qur'an (like surah 27, The Ant). Then tell one thing Muslims believe about the person in the story.

ch.t: Bismillah and Alhamdulillah
ch.bq: What words from the Qur'an do Muslims say every day, and what do they mean?
ch.talk: Yusuf says special words before and after he eats. Does your family say any special words at mealtime? What are they?

l.look: This translator uses the word "Beneficent." That is an old word for kind. What two things does this line say about God, as Muslims believe?
What do all the times Amira says Bismillah have in common? What is she about to do each time?
Yusuf says Alhamdulillah after he eats. How is his word like this line of the Qur'an?
The three friends use different words. What is the same about what the words mean?
A friend says "peace be upon you." What could you say back that is just as kind?

s.t: What the Qur'an Says to Do

l.look: What is one kind thing you could say to a parent or a grandparent today?
Which two things that the Qur'an says to do did this child do?

ch.t: Stories the Qur'an Tells
ch.bq: What stories does the Qur'an tell, and which ones do other families know too?
ch.talk: The ant was tiny, but she helped her friends. What did she do that was brave or kind?
ch.story: The Ant Who Warned Her Friends

l.look: Where did the boat stop when the water went down?
What did Yunus do when he was in the dark? What happened next?
Musa's mother was afraid. What was she told would happen to her baby?
Which way should the people walk now? How do you think they felt?

l.t: Ibrahim and Ismail Build the Kaaba
l.look: Who built the Kaaba, as the Qur'an tells it? What did they say while they built?
What did Maryam get from the tree and the stream? Why do you think the Qur'an tells this part?

s.t: The Ant and Stories We Share

l.look: The ant says the army would not know it stepped on the ants. Why does that matter in her warning?
Which of these surahs comes first in the Qur'an? Which comes last?

4.bq: How is the Qur'an put together, and how do Muslims keep it alive in voice, memory and art?
std: Use text features and search tools, such as key words and labels, to locate information quickly.
Determine the main idea of a text, explain how details support it, and summarize.
Teaching About Religion · expose not impose
Introduce a range of religious views without imposing any particular one.
4.write: Why do Muslims say the Qur'an is meant to be heard, not only read? Use two or three passages from this unit, such as 96:1-5 (Read!), 73:4 (recite slowly) and 97:1-3 (the Night of Power). Tell what each passage says and how Muslims act on it, such as tajwid, memorizing or Ramadan nights.

ch.t: 114 Surahs, 30 Parts
ch.bq: How is the Qur'an put together, and how do Muslims find their way around it?
ch.talk: Why might a family want thirty bookmarks in one book? What could dividing a book into equal parts help a reader do?

l.look: Which surah is the longest here? About how many times longer is it than the shortest?
A reader wants to finish the Qur'an in one week. Which division would help most? Why?

l.t: Why the Long Ones Come First
l.look: If you wanted to read the Qur'an in the order Muslims believe it came, where would you start? Why might a reader choose the book's own order instead?
Which group is bigger? Why might the Medinan surahs still fill many pages even though there are fewer of them?
Who is speaking, and to whom? What does the speaker ask for?
Pick two things the verse says about God. How might a Muslim reader feel saying this before sleep?
Pickthall used old English words. Put each of the four lines into your own words. What is the one idea all four lines share?
The teacher gives two reasons and then says nobody is certain. Why is it honest to say that? How is that different from making up an answer?

l.t: A Book Meant to Be Heard
l.look: Which word is repeated? What does the passage say the Lord teaches with?
What did each reader need to know to find the verse? What does this show about how the numbers help Muslims around the world?

ch.t: Reciting, Memorizing and Writing It Beautifully
ch.bq: Why do Muslims keep the Qur'an alive as sound, memory and art, not just as words on a page?
ch.talk: Nadia learned 98 verses by saying them a little at a time. Why might a person choose to learn a whole book by heart instead of just reading it?

l.look: Why might slow, clear reciting matter for a text that people learn by ear?
Why would a pause in the wrong place change the meaning? Give an example of an English sentence where a pause matters.
Why might teaching the Qur'an count as much as learning it, in this saying?
Who is "We" in this passage, as Muslims read it? What does the surah say about the night?
What does the teacher mean by "twenty copies, one Qur'an"? How is this like or unlike twenty copies of a school library book?
About how many years passed between the first standard copy and the printed Cairo edition? What changed on the page in that time?
Which page would be easier for a new reader? Which might be made to be admired? What does each choice say about who the page was for?
Why might a community choose a verse for its doorway instead of a picture? What might the repeating stars mean to the people who made them?
Which translation is the oldest? How many years passed between Sale and Pickthall?
The verse gives a reason for Arabic. What is it? How do Muslims who do not speak Arabic handle this today?

5.t: The Life of the Prophet as Context
5.bq: How does knowing the story of Muhammad's life help a reader understand the Qur'an?
std: Ask questions about people and groups who shaped important historical changes and continuities.
Describe a character's traits, motives and feelings and how the character's actions move the events.
Teaching About Religion · educate not promote or denigrate
Present every tradition fairly, neither advancing nor disparaging religion.
5.write: The Qur'an says not to push away the orphan (93:9–10), and it says God made people into nations and tribes so they could know one another (49:13). Pick one of these passages. Tell what it says. Then explain how one event from Muhammad's life, as Muslims tell it, helps a reader understand it.

ch.t: Mecca: The Message and the Hard Years
ch.bq: What did the first Muslims in Mecca hear, and why was it hard for them to stay?
ch.talk: Why do you think Muslim tradition remembers Bilal so well, when he began as an enslaved man with no power?

l.look: What might a boy who lived in Mecca learn just from watching caravans come and go?
A camel walks about 40 kilometers a day. About how many days was the trip from Mecca to Yathrib?
How are these two ways of telling the story different? What is each writer trying to do?
The first word is "Read." Why might that word matter so much to Muslims?
Muhammad was an orphan himself. How might that change the way he heard these words?
The first Muslims were very different ages. Why might that matter for a new group?
Why might the shop owner be angry? Which reason is about money, and which is about pride?
Why might Ja'far have chosen a surah about Maryam to recite to a Christian king?

l.t: The Boycott and the Sad Year
l.look: About how many years passed between the first words in the cave and the move to Yathrib?
The ayah does not name Jerusalem. How do you think Muslims came to read it that way?

ch.t: Medina: The Hijra and a Community
ch.bq: How did a small group of Muslims from Mecca become a community with its own city, rules and book?
ch.talk: What does it tell you about a town when its people rename it after one person who moved there?
ch.story: The City That Changed Its Name

l.look: Why do you think the meeting had to be secret? What were the people from Yathrib risking?
Look at the gaps. Why does year 1000 AH not land on the year 1622?
Both men acted well. What did each one do right? What might you do in each role?
Which of these rules do you think was hardest to keep? Why?
Why might facing the same place, wherever you are, matter to a community that is spread out?
The ayah says people before the Muslims also fasted. Which other groups fast? Why might the verse mention them?
How many years passed between the hijra and the return to Mecca? What happened in between?
Which friend do you agree with, and why? What does Surah 48 suggest?
Why do you think Muslim tradition remembers that Muhammad forgave his old enemies that day?

s.t: The Last Years and the Book

l.look: What does this ayah say makes one person better than another? What does it say does not?
Why might Abu Bakr have chosen this ayah to read on the day Muhammad died?
What could go wrong with each way alone? Why might using both be safer?

6.bq: What stories does the Qur'an tell about the prophets, and how do Jews, Christians and Muslims each read them?
std: Recount fables, folktales and myths from diverse cultures and explain the central message.
Compare how stories, myths and traditional literature from different cultures treat similar themes and events.
Teaching About Religion · inform not conform
Inform students about beliefs without asking them to conform to any.
6.write: Pick one prophet from this unit: Nuh, Ibrahim, Yusuf, Musa or Isa. Answer: How does the Qur'an tell this prophet's story, and how is the Bible's telling alike or different? Cite two or three passages by surah and ayah (for example, 12:92) or by Bible book and chapter (for example, Genesis 22). Explain what each text says and how Muslims, Jews or Christians read it.

ch.t: Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim and Yusuf
ch.bq: How does the Qur'an tell the stories of the early prophets, and how are they like the Bible's stories?
ch.talk: Why do you think the father tells Yusuf to keep his dream a secret from his brothers?
ch.story: Eleven Stars, the Sun and the Moon

l.look: Which of these surahs comes closest to the front of the book? Which comes near the end?
Which way of telling would you use to teach a lesson? Which way would you use to share the whole story?
What does God teach Adam before the angels bow? Why might that matter in the story?
Name one thing the two tellings share and one thing that is different.
What does the son think will save him? What does Nuh say will save people?
What did Ibrahim want the people to notice about their idols?
Why might the same story have a different son's name in two books? What does each book keep the same?

l.t: Building the Kaaba, and Eid al-Adha
l.look: Which part of Eid al-Adha connects to the story of Ibrahim's test? Which part helps other people?
Who is telling the story to whom, according to the surah's opening?
Which of these numbers also appears in the Bible's telling of Joseph in Genesis 37 and 41?
Yusuf had the power to punish his brothers. What did he choose instead, and why do you think the Qur'an ends the story this way?

ch.t: Musa, Maryam, Isa and Muhammad
ch.bq: How does the Qur'an tell about Musa, Maryam, Isa and Muhammad, and what does it say about Jews and Christians?
ch.talk: Why do you think Ja'far chose the surah about Maryam to read to a Christian king?
ch.story: A Surah Read to a King

l.look: Which person is different in the two tellings? What stays the same?
Why did Musa first go toward the fire? What did he find instead?
Which prophet is named far more than the others? Why might Musa's story be told so often?
What did Zakariya notice, and what did Maryam say about it?
Name two things that are different in the two tellings, and one thing both books share.

l.t: Isa, the Messiah, in the Qur'an
l.look: Sort the sentences: which beliefs are shared, and which belong to just one religion? Use "Muslims believe" or "Christians believe" when you answer.

l.t: Jews and Christians in the Qur'an
l.look: What does this verse tell Muslims to say about God when they talk with Jews and Christians?
Which of these books do Jews read? Which do Christians read? Which is read by Muslims only?
What does a seal do to a letter? How do Muslims use that picture to explain this verse?
Where would each of the three students stop? Which names would all three point to?

7.bq: What does the Qur'an ask of Muslims, in belief and in daily life, and where in the book does each teaching come from?
std: Determine the main idea of a text, explain how details support it, and summarize.
NCSS 1 · Culture
How people create, learn, share and adapt culture, and how cultures compare.
Teaching About Religion · study not practice
Teach about religious practices without having students take part in them.
7.write: What does the Qur'an say a good person does? Pick two or three passages from this unit, such as 17:23–24 on parents, 2:177 on giving, 31:13–19 on Luqman's advice or 2:185 on fasting. For each, tell what the passage says in your own words, and how Muslims put it into practice.

ch.t: One God, and Being Good
ch.bq: What does the Qur'an say about God, and about how a person should treat others?
ch.talk: If you could give one piece of advice to a younger child, what would it be, and why?

l.look: In your own words, what does tawhid mean, and what did it change about Mecca?
"Begetteth" is an old word for "has a child." Which of the four lines says God has no children?
Which is bigger: the number of surahs or the number of names? By how many?
The passage names one thing not to do and several things to do. List them.
Why do you think the Qur'an treats a small cheat on a scale as a big wrong?
Count the groups of people this ayah says to give to. Who is on the list?
Which student is boasting without saying a word? What could he do differently?
What does Luqman call his son? What does that tell you about how he is speaking?
"Subdue thy voice" means keep your voice low. Why might a wise father end his advice with this?
How might a person act differently if they believed every word was being written down?

l.t: The Day of Judgment and Paradise
l.look: What three things does this description of paradise mention? Why might rivers matter to people in a desert?

ch.t: Prayer, Fasting and the Pillars in the Qur'an
ch.bq: What do Muslims do because of the Qur'an, and where in the book do those practices come from?
ch.talk: Hana's family found out about Ramadan from the sky and from a phone. What is one thing your family waits for and gets ready for each year?

l.t: Five Pillars Hold Up a House
l.look: Which pillar is done most often? Which is done least often?
Which half of the shahada is about God, and which half is about Muhammad? Why do Muslims say both are needed?
In Chicago, the qibla is roughly toward the northeast. Why is it the same direction for a whole city, but different for a city in India?
If a family saved eight hundred coins, how many would zakat be? Why do you think the share is the same for everyone who pays?
The ayah gives a rule and then two exceptions. What are they? What reason does it give at the end?
Why do you think everyone on the hajj dresses the same? What lesson do Muslims take from it?
List the four parts of the body the ayah names. What does it say to do if there is no water?
How are the three days alike? How is the Muslim Friday different from the Jewish Sabbath?
If Eid al-Fitr was on April 1 this year, about when would it be next year?
What four things does the passage forbid? What does it say about a person who has no other food?

s.t: A Day, a Year, a World

l.t: A Muslim Child's Day and Year
l.look: Which prayers would fall during a school day in Chicago in winter? Which in summer, when the sun sets late?

l.t: Muslims in Chicago and the World
l.look: Which region has the most Muslims? Does that surprise you? Why might people guess a different region?

8.bq: How is the Qur'an built, and how did a text spoken aloud in Arabia become the book Muslims read and recite today?
std: Analyze how events and developments connect within their wider historical setting.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text, including terms specific to history and society.
Describe how a text presents information, such as in order, by comparison or by cause.
Teaching About Religion · academic not devotional
Study religion as an academic subject that describes beliefs and practices without leading worship.
8.write: How does the Qur'an's own description of itself fit with the history of how it was written down? Cite Qur'an 96:1–5, 15:9 and 73:4 (Pickthall, 1930), and the report of Zayd ibn Thabit in al-Bukhari. Explain what each text says, and how a Muslim reader and a historian each read the story of the text's preservation.
rooms: How to read a sacred text — the room

ch.t: Surah, Ayah, Juz': Order, Names and Style
ch.bq: How is the Qur'an put together, and why does its order and sound matter to the people who read it?
ch.talk: Dario said the short surah felt like a song and the long one felt like a speech. What might make a chapter feel one way or the other?

l.look: Surah 1 is at the front but is tiny. What does that tell you about the 'longest to shortest' pattern?
Why might a memorable word make a better name than a summary for a chapter that people learn by heart and recite aloud?

l.t: Parts for Reading: Juz' and Hizb
l.look: Which of these divisions follow meaning, and which follow length? How can you tell?
Each line begins with 'when.' What does this repeated pattern do to the listener, and what is the passage building toward?
The oath is one line, the claim is one line, and the exception is one line. What is the surah saying keeps a person out of 'loss'?
Which surah would tradition label Meccan and which Medinan? Name two clues in each that point to your answer.
Pick any gift a person enjoys daily. If this question followed it, how would the question change the way you think about the gift?
Name the picture and then state the idea behind it in one plain sentence. What makes the spider a good choice for the point?
Pickthall prints the letters with periods and no translation. What choices did he have, and why might he have chosen this one?
What does each translator gain and lose by writing 'Allah' or 'God,' and 'worlds' or 'all creatures'? Which would you choose for a classroom, and why?
Surah 2 is first in length but 87th in this list. Surah 110 is near the end of the book and is listed last. What pattern do you see between length and date?

ch.t: From Voice to Page: Collection, Script and Tajwid
ch.bq: How did words first spoken aloud in Arabia become the written Qur'an that Muslims recite today, and how do we know?
ch.talk: Radiocarbon dating tells us when the animal died, not when the words were written. What else would you want to know before saying how old the text on the pages is?
ch.story: Two Pages Older Than Anyone Thought

l.look: The passage opens with a command to read and then praises teaching by the pen. What does that pairing suggest about voice and writing in the Qur'an's own view of itself?
What are the strengths and the risks of keeping a text in memory and in scattered writing at the same time? Which risk would worry you most?
Zayd says the task felt heavier than moving a mountain. What would have made it so hard, given how the text was kept until then?
How many years passed between the Prophet's death and the standard copy? Why might that gap matter to a historian, and why might it not to a Muslim reader?
A range is not a date. What is the earliest and latest the Birmingham skin could be from, and why is that both exciting and limiting?
Suppose you found this page. What would you conclude about how the early text was kept, and what would you be careful NOT to conclude from one page?
Who could read the early bare script well, and who could not? What does that tell you about who the first written copies were for?
The letters are the same and the vowel differs. How does that one small difference show why vowel marks and chains of teachers both matter?
Why might a tradition that values exact sound build a whole set of rules from a verse that says 'recite in measured tones'?
Nearly 400 years separate the first attempt and the Cairo edition. What reasons in the reading explain why Muslims were slow to accept printed copies?
Muslims read this verse as a promise that the text is preserved. A historian would describe the preservation without the promise. Write one sentence in each voice.

9.t: Seerah: Mecca, Medina and the Occasions of Revelation
9.bq: How does knowing when, where and why a verse was revealed change the way its readers understand it?
std: Analyze how events and developments connect within their wider historical setting.
Explain the several causes and effects of past events and developments.
Analyze how a primary source and a secondary source on the same topic relate to each other.
Teaching About Religion · aware not accepting
Build students' understanding of religions without pressing them to accept any one.
9.write: Does knowing the occasion of a verse widen or narrow its meaning? Choose one verse from this unit (2:256, 2:190, 9:5 or 80:1–2), give its reported occasion, cite two other passages that bear on it (for example 9:4 and 9:6, or 22:39–40), and explain how at least two readers, such as al-Tabari and a modern scholar, have read it.

ch.t: Arabia Before Islam and the Meccan Period
ch.bq: What was Mecca like around the year 600, and how does that world help us read the earliest surahs?
ch.talk: Why would a reputation for honesty matter so much in a city with no courts? What does that tell you about how people in Mecca would first have judged a new message?

l.t: A Land of Tribes and Trade
l.look: A caravan traveled about 20 miles a day. Roughly how many days would it take to go from Mecca to Damascus? Why would such a trip need protection?
Which parts of that message would each listener already recognize, and which parts would be new or hard for each of them to accept?
What two things does this surah say the Lord of the House gave Quraysh? How does that connect to what you learned about Mecca's trade and truce?
About how many years passed between Muhammad's death and Ibn Ishaq's sira? Why might historians and believers weigh that gap differently?
What problem did this solution solve, and what does the story want the listener to think about Muhammad's character? Why might a historian call this a 'pious story'?

l.t: The Cave and the First Words
l.look: Which word is repeated, and what three things does the passage say about God? Why might a message that begins this way have been heard as a message about learning?
The surah earlier reminds the Prophet that he was once an orphan himself. How does that change the way you read these commands?

l.t: Boycott, Abyssinia and the Year of Sorrow
l.look: Why might the Muslims have chosen Surah 19 to recite to a Christian king? What does the story about the line say about how early Muslims wanted their relationship with Christians to be remembered?

l.t: One God and Nothing Beside Him
l.look: The surah begins with 'Say.' Who is being told to say this, and to whom? List the four claims it makes in your own words.

l.t: Judgment and Justice for the Weak
l.look: According to this surah, how can you tell whether someone truly holds their religion? What does that say about what 'religion' means here?
The verse does not name Jerusalem, Buraq or the seven heavens. Where does each of those details come from, and why does it matter to know that?

l.t: What Historians Can and Cannot Confirm
l.look: Which of these witnesses come from within Muhammad's lifetime or just after it? What can each one confirm, and what can it not?

ch.t: Medina, the Community and the Occasions of Revelation
ch.bq: How did the move to Medina change the Muslim community, and how does knowing the occasion of a verse change the way it is read?
ch.talk: If you knew that a verse was first spoken to settle an argument about dates in a market, would you read it differently than if you only had the words? What might you notice, and what might you miss?

l.look: Subtract 622 from each year to find the rough year AH. Why might Umar have chosen the hijra rather than the first revelation as year one?
What does the agreement ask each group to share, and what does it let each group keep separate? Why might that arrangement have appealed to a town torn by feuds?
What does this building tell you about how the early community saw the line between religious life and everyday life? Compare it with a house of worship you know.
How did the size of the forces change from Badr to the Trench? Why might tradition have preserved exact-sounding numbers, and why do historians treat them with care?

l.t: The Trench and the Jewish Tribes
l.look: What does each sentence leave out or assume? Which one would you want in a public-school textbook, and why?

l.t: Hudaybiyyah and the Return to Mecca
l.look: Some reports place this verse around the time of Hudaybiyyah, when Muslims feared being attacked during pilgrimage. What limit does the verse set, and who is it addressed to?
According to this verse, why do different nations and tribes exist, and what makes a person noble? How does that match the reported words of the farewell sermon?
Read the passage without knowing the story: who could 'he' be? Now read it with the report about Ibn Umm Maktum. What changes?
Read the two sentences together. What reason does the second sentence give for the first? How does the reported occasion about the Ansar fathers fit, or not fit, that reason?
How does the meaning of 9:5 shift when 9:4 and 9:6 are read with it? Whom does each reader think the verse is about?

l.t: Medinan Themes: Law, Family and the People of the Book
l.look: What pattern do you see between where a surah was revealed and its length? Why might a community in Medina need longer passages than a preacher in Mecca?

10.bq: What does the Qur'an teach about God and about how to live, and why does the context of a verse change what its readers take from it?
std: Determine a source's central ideas and give an accurate summary free of prior opinions.

l.look: Each of the four lines says something God is or is not. List the four claims in your own words. Which one answers the idea of "daughters of God" that Muslim tradition says Meccans held?
Which translator keeps two separate words for the two Arabic names, and which one folds them into one? What is gained or lost in each choice?
List every claim the verse makes about God. Which claims are about power, and which are about knowledge? Why might a reader recite this verse before sleeping?
What does each text say happened after the six days? How does each tradition explain the word "rested" or its absence? What would a reader miss by reading only one text?
Each line asks about how something came to be. Rewrite the four questions as one statement that begins "Because...". What does the verse expect its hearers to conclude?
Using only these three verses, explain the difference between an angel and a jinn in the Qur'an. Why does it matter to the story of Adam that Iblis was a jinn and not an angel?
Muhammad is named far less than Musa. What reason do Muslim scholars give? What does the list suggest about the stories the Qur'an's first hearers already knew?
Which earlier book does the Qur'an name most? Given that Musa is also the prophet named most, what might that say about who the Qur'an's first hearers were talking with?
The verse chooses the smallest weight its hearers could picture. What claim about judgment does that choice make? How might this passage sound to a poor listener in Mecca and to a rich one?
How can both readers use the same verse? Does 9:72 support one reading more than the other, or does it hold both? Explain with the verse's order of ideas.

ch.story: One Verse, Then the Verse Before It

l.look: The verse lists three people a witness might want to protect. Why those three? What would be hard about obeying this verse in a society built on family and tribe?
The verse joins worship of God to kindness to parents in one sentence. What does that pairing suggest? Why name so small a sound as "uff" instead of a large wrong?
The surah defines denying religion by actions toward other people, not by beliefs. Then it criticizes people who pray. What point is the surah making about the link between worship and conduct?
The Qur'an names the receivers but not the rate. Where does the rate come from? Why might the rate on rain-watered crops be higher than on irrigated ones?
State each reader's argument in one sentence. What does each reader do with the verse the other one stresses? Is this a disagreement about words, about history, or about both?
Muslim commentators say these verses came in this order over several years. Why might a rule come in steps rather than all at once? What does each step add?
The verse gives one permission and one limit in a single sentence. Name each. How does 2:192, which says to stop if they stop, add a second limit?
The second sentence gives a reason for the first. What is the reason? How does the story al-Tabari reports about children in Medina fit the words?
The verse names an exception before it names the rule. What is the exception? How does the Mishnah's version (Sanhedrin 4:5) compare, and why do Muslim scholars say the likeness is expected?

The passage promises a result and then names a cost. What is the result, and what is the cost? Compare it with 42:40, which allows an equal response and then praises forgiveness. Do the two verses agree?
All these scholars died more than a century after Muhammad's death in 632. What does that gap tell you about the difference between the Qur'an and fiqh?
Which reader uses abrogation? Which uses occasions of revelation? Which reads the whole book? Which tool would you want a reader to use first, and why?

How could one verse like this lead to whole libraries of reports about the Prophet's daily life?
Muslim scholars read this verse as a warrant for tafsir. What does the verse ask its readers to do?

l.t: Ibn Kathir and Qur'an by Qur'an
l.look: How many centuries separate the first and last of these commentators? What might a later commentator know that an earlier one could not?

l.look: This verse is one reason Muslims keep the Qur'an in Arabic. What is gained by keeping one language, and what problem does it create for readers who do not know Arabic?

What do the first three schools have in common with the last two? What was taught in each, and who paid for it?

Can a translation made to argue against a book still be useful for studying it? What would you check in each translation before trusting it?
How long was the gap between the first Latin and the first English-from-Arabic version? What changed in 1930?
Some scholars read Omar's choice of this surah as a quiet statement about who truly rules. What in the surah's opening supports that reading? What other reasons might he have had?
What did the book mean to each man? What does it tell you that a copy bought for study became a symbol of belonging?

Match each scene to a practice from this unit: recitation, tafsir, interfaith reading. Which of the three would have surprised a scholar in Baghdad in the year 900, and which would he have recognized at once?

The book's order is 1, 93, 96, 103, 112. The traditional order of revelation is different. What does the gap between the two orders tell you about how the Qur'an is arranged?
Each verse rules something out. Name what each one excludes. Why might a text about God be built mostly from what God is not?
Pick one surah and name the single verse where it turns. If you removed that verse, what would happen to the surah's meaning?

What does the shirt mean in each scene? How does the surah use one object to mark the story's turn from loss to restoration?

Muslim tradition reports that Muhammad quoted this verse when he entered Mecca in 630 and pardoned his former enemies. Why would this line fit that moment?

What is the same in the two scenes, and what has changed? How does each text explain why the old man cannot speak?
